title: Buster Smith, Charlie Parker's idol, and trips to Kansas City
summary: Edison says Buster Smith played Parker-like lines before Parker and describes driving from St. Louis to Kansas City.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Oh, sure it was. He came -- he's the one wrote "One O'Clock Jump," you know. And he was playing like Charlie Parker even before Charlie Parker even thought there was a style he was playing. Bird used to go around and listen to him at the place called the Kansas City Bar-be-que. Used to listen to him intently because he was playing the same thing that Charlie Parker was playing that the people -- you know, that the Bird -- of course, Bird added to it, naturally. But his idol was Buster Smith.
Yeah, I've heard, you know, records that Buster made 10 years ago or something, and the tone was --
Sure, that's right. I mean, he played the

chords, you know. He would lead in a melody on something on the blues like Charlie Parker. He was the greatest taker of the blues chords and making something out of them, you know. And Buster Smith was playing like that in those days, you know. Because I used to go from St. Louis to Kansas City on weekends, you know, just to hang out. And, oh, he was fantastic. He was fantastic, alto player.
How far is St. Louis from Kansas City?

No, we'd drive down. We'd drive down. Oh, it was a thrill to go down there, you know. Then they would all -- a lot of the guys would come to St. Louis because there was a lot happening in St. Louis at the time, too. Harold Baker was playing nightclubs.
